target_customer: Developers and business analysts who wanted to run big data analysis and build data apps without managing infrastructure; at the 2014 relaunch, developers wanting distributed computing without specialist engineers.
problem: Analyzing large datasets required stitching together cloud infrastructure, data acquisition and cleaning, and distributed algorithms, which was out of reach for most business users and small teams.
business_model: Usage-based cloud data platform (pay for compute consumed), with reusable components and bundled datasets
product_category: Cloud data analysis platform (big data PaaS)

founders.name: Jake Quist
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch 2011 says the founders were Google engineers who used internal data analysis tools.

founders.name: Tyler Neylon
founders.background_notes: Listed as founder and CTO on the YC page; no further background found.

founders.name: Peter Harrington
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page as founder and chief scientist.

founders.name: Roger Huffstetler
founders.background_notes: Named co-founder and president in the 2014 TechCrunch relaunch article; not on the YC page.

technical_complexity.rationale: Building a multi tenant cloud platform with automatic scaling, a crawled copy of the web, and distributed processing was heavy infrastructure work for a two to four person team in 2011 and 2012.

defensibility.rationale: The crawled web dataset and components were a modest asset, but the platform pattern was reproducible by large cloud vendors, and the product shifted twice, which diluted any lock in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: In 2014 Google Cloud Dataflow and Amazon Kinesis were announced as stream and data processing services, which the company itself compared against at its August 2014 relaunch.

market_need_then: The 2011 launch article says existing big data tools were niche, mostly for large enterprises, and unsatisfactory for business users, while Google trained engineers had seen the value of internal analysis tools. Demand evidence beyond that was not found.

branding.domain_note: Used zillabyte.com (exact .com); no acquisition story found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Developer facing, 'Build apps, not infrastructure'; earlier consumer style framing as 'Pandora for sales leads'.

brand_strength.rationale: No press on the brand itself, no community or merch found, and the name outlived neither of its two positionings. Coverage was limited to TechCrunch launch and relaunch stories.

pivots.from: Sales lead recommendation app described as a Pandora for sales leads
pivots.to: General cloud platform for data analysis and distributed computing for developers
pivots.why: Building the lead product had required a distributed infrastructure layer, so the company chose to sell the platform itself.

outcome_analysis: Zillabyte launched in stealth in late 2011 as a big data platform for business users, joined YC in Winter 2012, then reframed itself as a sales lead product and relaunched in August 2014 as a developer data platform just as Google and Amazon announced comparable services. The YC directory now lists the company as inactive and its founders as former founders, but no post-mortem or acquisition notice was found, so the cause of the shutdown is not public. The failure factors reflect a plausible reading of the pivots and cloud vendor entry, not a stated cause.
notes: Company site zillabyte.com returned HTTP 503 at fetch time. CB Insights snippet reports about $2.22M over three rounds (Jan 2012, Apr 2012, Jun 2013 seed of about $2.2M with Menlo Ventures, plus Threshold, Boldstart, KEC Ventures, Kevin Donahue named as investors) but it was seen only in an aggregator snippet and is unverified, so no rounds are recorded. TechCrunch in Sept 2011 said the company was self funded. No dated competitor sources from around the Winter 2012 batch were found; the 2011 article named no competitors and the later rivals (Infer, Lattice Engines, Mintigo, Kinesis, Dataflow) are from 2014. Searches for a shutdown or acquisition returned nothing about Zillabyte. Update: the rounds now recorded rest on a single database (CB Insights, which reports $2.22M over three rounds; the 2013 seed of about $2.2M is the only amount given, the Jan 2012 and Apr 2012 rounds have no stated amount). Kando lists the same June 2013 seed with Menlo Ventures, KEC Ventures and DFJ, so the investor list differs by database. A cross-check search found no press release or filing.
